Or they ask that they be given the same terms as were given to Alberta and Saskatchewan; in other words, what is asked by our friends on the other side of the House is not only that they be given an addition to their territory, but that the financial terms upon which Manitoba was organized in 1869 should be absolutely and completely revised and that new terms should be given to them altogether. They do not ask simply that they should have the lands in the new territory, but that the whole terms of confederation, under which they have been in this Dominion for forty years, should be revised and that new conditions altogether should be made. Is that reasonable? Here is the province of Manitoba asking, and I think asking with good cause, to have their territory extended. Well, then you and I, in the simplicity of our souls, would suppose that they would ask for the land in that territory. No, they are not content to ask us to give them the land in the territory, but they say that we should revise our whole policy of the last forty years of keeping the control of the lands in the hands of this Dominion, set that policy aside and give to Manitoba the lands, not only in the new territory, but in the whole province. That is the position taken by Manitoba, is it not? I ask if there is, for such a position, any ground that can be taken upon this request for new territory. If the province of Manitoba is entitled to have the land of the whole province vested in the government of Manitoba it is not in consequence of this demand for new territory. It must be done, whether the territory is extended or not, but I submit that it is simply absurd to pretend that as a consequence of the extension of the territory of Manitoba the land should he given to the province, not in the new territory alone, but in the whole territory of the province. I can understand that the province of Manitoba has a good case when it says: If you give us new territory give us the means of administering it. We are prepared to do that, and that is what we did under the resolution of 1908, but Manitoba says: No, we will not do that; the parliament of Canada was wrong in 1869. When the government of Sir John Macdonald incorporated the province of Manitoba and brought it into the Dominion, parliament u'as wrong in keeping to the Dominion the lands of Manitoba. That is altogether another proposition, and that is a proposition that for my part, I say it to our friends, and I say it to our foes on the other side, to the members from Ontario, from Saskatchewan, from Quebec, and from all the provinces, that we are not prepared to reverse the policy which was adopted in 1869 by the government of Sir John Macdonald, and which has been followed ever since by all successive governments. Now, Sir, I am prepared to meet my hon. friend upon this, that Manitoba is entitled to compensation either in land or money in the new territory which is to he annexed, and the amount of compensation must be such as will give Manitoba the facilities and the means of administering that new territory. I am prepared to meet them upon this, and that is the reason we are asking for a new negotiation of these terms, because if Messrs. Roblin, Rogers and Campbell ask us-I will not discuss what took place in the conference-but if they ask that we should revise the whole terms of Manitoba, not only with respect to the territory to be annexed, but with respect to the whole province nobody should be sur-

prised if we could not agree, but I hope that in a new conference, Mr. Roblin and his ministers will understand that we are to deal with new territory and nothing else.
My hon. friend, in his resolution, also asks that we shall not only give to Manitoba the lands in the whole province, but; that we shall give to Manitoba the terms, that we have given to Alberta and Saskat-, chewan. That is to say, that we should revise the financial terms which have been given to Manitoba. Well, Sir, I have only to observe that these financial terms have been revised again and again and again; they have been revised four or five times already. The last time they were revised was in 1907, by a resolution adopted by this House on the 25th of March of that year, and since embodied in an imperial statute which has fixed for all time the terms andj conditions and financial arrangements which are to exist between the government of the Dominion and the provincial governments. The resolution which was passed in this House on the 25th of March, 1907, was in the form of a petition to His Majesty the King, asking that the financial terms which had been fixed at confederation for the provinces, should be revised for Manitoba as well as for all the other provinces; and Tevised they were. The petition went on to say:
Me pray that your Majesty may be graciously pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the imperial parliament at its present eesswn, repealing the provisions of section lls ot the British North America Act, 1867, aforesaid, and substituting therefor the scale ol payments above set forth, which shall be a hnal and unalterable settlement of the amounts to be paid yearly to the several provinces of the Dominion for their local purposes and the support of their governments and legislatures.
This House so determined in 1907, and it is embodied in an imperial statute, and forms the law and the constitution at the present time. As far as that goes, to me it is final. But again, I repeat, as far as new territory is concerned which may be added to the province of Manitoba, it is fair and reasonable that compensation should be made to the province, either in land or money, to enable it to administer civil government for that territory, and that territory alone; and if my hon. friend with his friends come to Ottawa and have a new conference with ns on this question, we are ready to meet them; and if it is our good fortune to come to a satisfactory agreement, we shall be only too happy to introduce legislation to give effect to the result of the negotiations which may take place between us. The province of Manitoba, for the purpose of bringing about a settlement of this question, which had been delayed by the inaction of this government for so many years, yielded a portion of its claims and accepted the limited extension of its boundaries proposed to this parliament by the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues. In that Tegard, I would like to make one observation and ask one question of hon. gentlemen in this House. The Prime Minister has taken strong ground upon the position that it is not a proper course_ for the government to present the financial terms to parliament by resolution, and then forward them to the government of Manitoba for its acceptance or rejection. I would like to ask any man in this House possessing ordinarv reasoning faculties to tell me what the difference is between presenting the boundaries to parliament by resolution and then leaving them to be accepted or rejected bv the legislature of Manitoba, on the one hand, and_ on the other hand, presenting the financial terms to parliament by resolution, and then leaving them to be accepted or rejected by the legislature of Manitoba? If there is any reasonable difference of

principle between the two courses, I will be glad to take my seat and let the Prime Minister explain what it is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The difference is very obvious. There was a dispute between Manitoba, Ontario and Saskatchewan as to what should be the limits. We had a conference on the subject, and we had to decide on our best judgment, since they could not agree.

There it is in a'nutshell. Because there was a disagreement between this government and the government of Manitoba in respect of the boundaries, because the government of Manitoba insisted upon certain territory which this government thought should go to Ontario and to Saskatchewan, the government brought its proposals by resolution into parliament and passed it. There is an exactly similar difference of opinion between this government and the government of Manitoba with regard to the financial terms. Why, then, should not the government of Canada follow exactly the same course-bring in its proposals, have them embodied in a resolution of parliament, and then leave them to be accepted or -rejected? There is no difference between the two positions.

Guelph armouries, $2,250.

My hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) is in his place, and will be able to give some additional information, if it is required, as to the necessity for the room which was erected over the gun-shed. I may first say that a request was made by the Department of Militia for this building on April 12, 1907, in the following communication :
To the Deputy Minister of Public Works.
Sir,-I have the honour to state that, if possible, this department would like to have an additional storey built over the gun shed which you are now constructing at Guelph, Ontario.
It is, therefore, requested that you will have your chief architect look into this question, with a view to making the portion over the gun shed into a drill room, and let me know if it is feasible under the present construction.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
EUG. FISET, Colonel.
Deputy Minister, Militia and Defence.
On the 12th March, 1908, the following letter was received:
Proposed additional story Guelph gun shed. Sir,-I have the honour to return, herewith, for action, the plans which you submitted to this department on the 30th January last, showing the proposed additional etory for the gun shed at Guelph.
These plans have been approved by this department with the addition of a doorway and steps between the Assembly Hall and passage on the first floor.
I shall be glad if you can have this small change carried into effect.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
E. F. JARVIS, Acting Deputy Minister. To the Deputy Minister,
Public Works Department,
Ottawa.
How much has the Guelph armoury cost the country to date?

I gave that when the item was under consideration before. Up to November 30, 1909, the total amount expended was $142,464.
Niagara Falls armoury, $50,000.

This is to make provision for the erection of an armoury in Niagara Falls, which has been asked for by the Department of Militia. As hon. gentlemen know, Niagara Falls is right on the boundary, and it is desirable not only that 'an armoury should be erected there, but that it should be one of adequate dimensions for the accommodation of the militia.
This is to commence the work, is it?
Yes.
What will be the total cost?	*
Ottawa Government Printing Bureau, building for storing type and supplies, $7,500.

This has been urged on our consideration for a very considerable time, and we have felt that the time has now arrived when it is necessary to provide for what is now asked. It is to erect a building to store type and supplies at the Printing Bureau.
It would be interesting to know how much printing we are paying for outside of the Printing Bureau.

My hon. friend would not expect me to give the information upon this vote, because it is not in my department. If my memory serves me right a motion was made for a return by the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) and that'retum was brought down.

Partially.
Ottawa departmental buildings-improvements in lavatories, plumbing, etc., $10,000.
This is for the improvements that we are making in the buildings.
Is an improvement going to be made in the ventilation?
It is difficult to improve that. I think the ventilation is all right.
In this room?
Yes.

If the hon. gentleman thinks that the ventilation in this particular Chamber is all right he is very much in the minority amongst gentlemen in this House. I think it is the universal opinion that the ventilation of this Chamber is absolutely wretched. We work in other parts of the building, and we seem all right, but when we stay here for three or four hours at a time we get sick headaches. It has been that way for two or three years.
We had experts here who looked into the question of ventilation.
They did not stay here as long as we do.
There are 200 of us in this Chamber, and there are at times a good many people in the galleries as well, and it is impossible to keep the atmosphere absolutely pure under these circumstances.

Thar is a different thing. If it is impossible to do it, that is one thing, but what I was protesting against was the statement, that it was all right. I want to register my opinion that it is not all right.
I meant relatively.

We can work in the Railway Committee room, or in other parts of the building, and we seem to be all right, but when we remain in this Chamber for three or four hours we get headaches from the bad air that we are breathing. I think that is the case with nine-tenths of the members who stay in the House for a few hours at a time. It may be that there are so many of us in the Chamber that it is difficult for the hon. gentleman's engineers and architects to deal with the matter, but I think it ought to be possible to find a remedy, and if it is not we should get a larger chamber, because the conditions existing at the present time are injurious to our health.

To find the remedy we should know the cause. The minister says that his experts have examined the chamber, and that there is nothing wrong about the ventilation. I take it that it is all right when there is no person in it. My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) says that when we work elsewhere we have no trouble from bad air, but that when we come into the House we are in trouble. It must be, if we are all right outside, and that there is no trouble but plenty of pure air in the Chamber when it is not occupied by the members, then it must be due to the fact that we are brought into contact with the government, and that they are responsible for the impurity of the air in it.

This aitemoon there were nine on this side of the House and fifteen on the other sound asleep when the right hon. First Minister was talking, and I do not think that he exercised a very soporific influence on the House.
That shows that the atmosphere was good.

That shows that the atmosphere was bad, that it was soporific. I do not like to blame any official, but when this new wing was constructed in which room 89 is located, with the exception of a few holes for windows, there was no provision made for ventilation.
Which is room 89?

The hole where the Conservative party is stored. I presume that the other rooms in the building are the same. There is not the first attempt at ventilation. The rooms were constructed the same as they were a thousand and fifty years before the birth of Christ.

It seems to me that the chief source of difficulty is the long hours that we put in in this chamber. We are required to meet here at eleven o'clock in the morning during the latter part of the session after perhaps spending an hour in committee, and we sit here until midnight with only a slight intermission, and there is very little opportunity for the engineers to ventilate the room. I think that is the great source of the trouble, and I am sure that we are making a terrible mistake in trying to overtake the business of the country in a shorter time at the expense of our health. I have realized that fact, and I am quite sure that others must have realized the same thing. To-day we have a motion to sit on Saturday. After sitting five days in the week we are now compelled to come back on Saturday at eleven o'clock, and put in time possibly until midnight. I think it is absolutely absurd, and that the government are making a mistake in asking members of this House to work such long hours in a room where there are 200 members and, as the Minister of Public Works has said, often full galleries consuming all the fresh air that can possibly be brought in by the fans or otherwise. We are certainly acting very indiscreetly in our own interests. I see no good purpose to be gained by it. We had better put in two weeks more, and save our health than rush through the session in a shorter period for the sake of getting home a little earlier.

If the minister would take a trip to one or two of the public schools in Ottawa or go to any second-class town in the country and examine the schools there he would see proper systems of ventilation in use by which the air in a room can be changed in a minute or a minute and a half. To tell us that it is impossible to ventilate a building such as this is childish on the part of those who are advising the minister.

I think it speaks rather well for the ventilation of this room that we are able to stay here, and feel so brisk.
I notice that on this side there is a very nice breeze circulating in the chamber.
There is now, but there was not this afternoon when the First Minister was talking.

I have been told by members who have been in the House for some years that in the last few sessions the ventilation has not been as good as it was previously. That may be due to the fact that the new wing has been opened, and that the system of ventilation has been interfered with by it. I do not think that the ventilation has been as good during the last two sessions as it was three or four vears ago.

Ottawa parliament grounds-driveway pavement, $21,000.

This is around the parliament buildings. It is to complete the work of reconstructing the pavements. We had to make a new driveway by reason of the erection of the additional wing, and we have been replacing the old driveway.
Mr. SPROULE What kind of pavement is being put down?
Bitulithic pavement.
What is it costing per yard??
$1.90 per square yard.
Is that not very high?
The deputy minister informs me it is quite cheap; $2.50 was the lowest tender which we got.
What concerns did you have tenders from?
The different paving concerns.
Cannot you give us the names?
I have not them here. This was some time ago.

But we should know who gave tenders, and from whom you asked tenders. I know something of the bitulithic paving, and we have as well paved streets in Halifax as you have in Ottawa, and they do not cost as much as $1.90 per yard. I understand this is the main street you are paving.

No, round the parliament grounds. It has nothing to do with a street. I would be glad to give my hon. friend information as to the cost of similar work done in 1905. The lowest tenderers were the Warren Bituminous Paving Company, of Toronto. We paid them $2.25 per square yard.
For paving round these parliament buildings?
That was street paving on Wellington street.

Will the minister tell us what the thickness of this pavement is? I notice that it is very much broken up, whether by frost or not I do not know. Down in front of the buildings there are great cracks nearly an inch wide.
My hon. friend has in mind the sidewalk.
No, the front of the building.
I think my hon. friend is mistaken, there are no cracks in it. The cracks are in the walk built some years ago 259J
They are right from the building to the steps.
I have not noticed the-cracks.

Would the hon. minister tell us if it is his intention to tear up the driveway at present round the grounds and replace it with this bitulithic pavement? We have now what I consider a pretty fair macadam roadway, and in my opinion a good macadam roadway is better than a bitulithic pavement in a park system of driveway. They are not to be compared, and with the use of oil, these macadam roadways are far better for driving than either asphalt or bitulithic. I think that with very little expense the surface of the present driveways could be made almost perfect.

If the hon. member will go down by the east block, he will see. the new pavement we have put in there. It is exceedingly good, and has excited very favourable comment, but alongside the west block there is no pavement. There is only an ordinary earth roadway, and we propose laying down this bitulithic pavement there and around the buildings wherever there is no pavement at present, or where it is worn out. I think it is all right for horses.
The hon. minister has not told us the thickness.
About 6 or 8 inches of concrete underneath and then li inches of asphalt on the top.
Why does not the hon. minister ask for tenders for this work?

We can do it more
cheaply by employing the men in our own department.
Are you sure about that?
Yes, that has been demonstrated.
How does my hon. friend get round the Act?

The Act expressly states that where, in the opinion of the minister, the work can be done more economically and better by day work, it can be done without calling for tenders. We have men in the employ of the department, and we have a foreman, of course, and we find it more economical to do this class of work under the direction of our own foreman and by employing labouring men by the day.
What Act does my hon. friend refer to?
The Public Works Act.

I would like to ask the minister again if he is bound to put in

this bitulithic pavement? It's surface is so hard that it is like glass. I think if the minister were to consult the wishes of the horse-drivers and those who use public -driveways, he would find that a macadam -or gravel roadway would be preferred to any new form of pavement, and we have already a foundation for a good gravel road there.

I think my hon. friend will agree with me that a great deal depends on whether the roadway is level or sloping. There is a great deal of wash on this hill, and it has been found impossible to keep an ordinary roadway in good condition. That is the reason why we are putting down the pavement. I have heard no complaint from horsemen from driving on the pavement which we have already constructed.

I will register a complaint now. There is only one means of safety in driving on a pavement of that kind, and that is by putting rubber boots on the horse. I know a good deal about the bitulithic pavement, and it has only one advantage that I can see, that is in regard to dust; but by sprinkling crude oil on macadamized roadways you can overcome the dust altogether and make a very satisfactory surface.

I entirely -concur in what the hon. -member for East Toronto says, and if the minister were to take the opinion of -men who have to drive, I think he would find that it is absolutely correct. In park systems, like that around Boston, where the roads are supposed to be the best in the world, you do not find such pavements, but you do find excellent macadamized roadways welL looked -after, and there is nothing better for a country like ours, with such extreme changes of temperature. A pavement such as we have here, if it becomes wet and suddenly freezes, is so slippery as to be dangerous to drive over, especially if it goes down hill.

We are hardly in a position to make a fair comparison as to the cost and quality of the pavement around this building with ordinary street pavements. The pavement on the -street i-s much deeper and ought to be more costly. If this pavement costs $1.90 a square yard and the street pavement costs from $2.25 to $2.50, I do not think there is much -evidence that -this costs less than the other, because this is lighter and is not so carefully put down. I believe that if a fair comparison were made, this would be found to be the dearer at the price stated.

I do not like to dispute the hon. minister's interpretation of the law, but I t-hink it is so plain that a laym-an can see that it provides, that any Mr. RUSSELL.
work costing more than $5,000 must be done by tender and contract.

My hon. friend is wrong, and my interpretation is that put On the Act by the Auditor General. Even if the amount is over $5,000, if in the opinion of the minister from the nature of the work it can be done more expeditiously -and economically by day labour, it can be done in that way.

I know that the opinion always entertained by the ex-minister of railways was that no work costing more than $5,000 could be done by day labour, except when a dam broke away or something of that kind happened.

I think I satisfied the ex-minister of railways that my view of the law was correct, and I have received a memorandum from the Auditor General confirming my view.
Ottawa parliament building-cleaning, painting and redecorating interior of senate chamber, $15,000.
This has been urgently asked for by the Speaker and other members of the Senate, and more especially the Committee on Internal Economy of the Senate.
Is it to be done by tender?

I am not sure whether it can be done by tender ot not. It will mean the renovating of the paintings in the panels of the Senate chamber and other work of that character, which it is somewhat difficult to do by tender.
Ottawa public buildings, Langevin block- new boilers and alterations in heating apparatus, $10,000.
The old boilers are worn out and it is necessary to replace them.
Does the department pay for the heating or is it done by contract?
We buy our own fuel and have our own men.
What kind of fuel?
Anthracite coal.
About what price does the department have -to pay for it?
We invite tenders for all the coal supplied for the different buildings.	-
Can the hon gentleman tell the annual cost of heating the Langevin block?

I cannot tell that. We could of course take the quantity of coal consumed and the wages paid to firemen

and labourers, and in that way get at the cost. This will come up later under the item for heating, and I will then have the information for my hon. friend as to the price paid for coal.
Ottawa fuel testing building, $1,000.

This is the balance required to pay for the building for testing peat fuel.
Parkhill public building-$10,0G0.

This is to complete the payments.
Port Arthur armoury-revote of $10,000, lapsed, $30,000.
This is a new building which has been pressed upon our attention. An armoury is very much needed at Port Arthur. In addition to the armoury there will be a drill hall.
How much will that cost?

When I was at Port Arthur I discussed the character of the building which would be necessary with the officers of the militia. The city is growing very rapidly, and the military spirit is excellent, and I think we should give them a good armoury and drill hall. I do not imagine that we can do it for less than $75,000 to $100,000. If we give them a drill hall as well, it will probably run over $100,000.
What about Fort William?

There they said they would be willing to wait for a little. We had hoped that one building would do for the two cities, but owing to the considerable distance between them, there did not seem to be any proper place where an armoury or drill hall could be constructed that would suit both cities.
What is the strength of the militia who will use this building?
The city is growing so fast that we cannot tell. It is the 96th Lake Superior regiment that is there at present.
What is the strength of that regiment?

I have no particulars about that.
Sarnia armoury-revote of $500, lapsed,
What is this going to cost?
We have not prepared the plans yet. Of course, we will confer with the Militia Department, but my hope is that it will not exceed $50,00.
What troops are there?

It is the headquarters of the 27th Lambton regiment, the St. Clair Borderers, ' G ' and ' H ' companies, and the headquarters also of the 14th Field Ambulance.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Toronto drill hall-additional accommodation for new corps and armouries, $20,000.
What new corps is to be accommodated in Toronto?

The medical corps.
Uxbridge public building-revote of $6,740, lapsed, $15,000.

How much will this cost? Mr. PUGSLEY. We hope to complete this for about $15,000.
Wallaceburg public building, $5,000.
What will be the total cost of this?
Probably about $20,000.
Does that include furnishings, fittings, heating and lighting?

It will include heating and lighting, but not furnishings.
Waterloo public building-revote of $2,970, lapsed, $20,000.
What will be the total cost of this building?

Waterloo is a very important place. The population even in 1901 was 3,500, and it is growing rapidly. There is a very large public revenue. This will be for a post office, customs and inland revenue. I think the cost of this building will run up to $35,000.
There is no customs there.
Perhaps this is for inland revenue and post office only. But it is a growing place and there is a large business.
And it is represented by a minister of the Crown.
Quite true. The revenue there is extraordinary for the size of the place. The inland revenue alone last year amounted to $509,000.
Not very surprising when you have there one of the largest distilleries in the country.
Surprising or not, it means a large business.
Tenders will be called for by public advertisement for this building, I suppose.

Yes.
Whitby public building-$15,000.
What is to be the total cost of this building?

It is estimated that th=>
total cost will be $41,645.86, including site" heating, electric wiring, furnishings, etc.'
Whitby is only a small place.
Well, Whitby is quite an important place. There is Whitby town and West Whitby, and the population of the two is considerably over 4,000. It is the county town, as well.
Is this building to serve the two places?
I think so.
What constituency is it in?
South Ontario.

Before we leave this item of Ontario public buildings, I would like to point out that the minister has been very generous to some counties. Take, for instance, the county of Wellington! Besides the armoury at Guelph, which the minister told us this afternoon would cost over $140,000, we find estimates here for public buildings for Elora, Fergus, Harris1-ton and Mount Forest.
They are not in the same riding.

But they are in the same county. Harriston and Mount Forest are in North Wellington, and Elora and Fergus in South Wellington. Here is one county getting four buildings. True, it is represented by two Liberals. To the victors belong the spoils-that is the principle on which the Minister of Public Works proceeds. And I do not know that I should find fault with him. Sarnia is given a public building-and that constituency is represented by a Liberal. Seaforth-also,
I think, is represented by a Liberal. I am almost afraid the minister made a mistake -Tilbury is given a public building; I am not sure whether that is represented by a Liberal or not.
It is.
And Tilsonburg?
That is in South Oxford.
Also represented by a Liberal. And Whitby, represented by a Liberal.
The hon. member (Mr. Henderson) passes over Toronto.
It was quite impossible for the minister to overlook Toronto. They are only reaching out the long arm trying to capture Toronto.
And Uxbridge, in North Ontario.
I suppose that was started before the last general election.
It is not started yet.
The amount was put in the estimates before the last general election.

It was one of these items carried over, I presume. I am not making a plea for the county of Halton. But here is a county that has never had a public building. I suppose it is the mistake made by the people in sending a representative who does not support the hon. gentleman.
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman says 'hear, hear.' He approves of that policy. The money spent on these public buildings is tire money of the people; Conservatives contribute to the revenue of the country just as well as Liberals, and I submit that to erect public buildings on political lines is hardly in keeping with what I would think the good judgment of the minister undeT ordinary circumstances would be. I think he has allowed himself to be carried away when he puts a public building in a small place like Elora with a population of 1,200, and in Fergus, Harriston and Mount Forest, four public buildings in one county m a year, and leaves other counties that never had a public building without any consideration. Does it not appear to the minister that there is something political an the whole matter? I do not know that I have any right to complain. The hon. gentleman thinks he has a right to serve his friends. Does he think it will require four public buildings in the county of Wellington to bring back two Liberal members at the next election? He must think there is some doubt about the result of the next election or he would not spend so much money in one county. The money belongs to the people and it is the duty of the minister to consider the necessities of the country, independent of political considerations. If the minister will frankly state that he is guided by politics in this matter I shall rest the matter there and not complain, but every district in the country has a right to some consideration in the distribution of public money whether it sends a supporter of the government or one not in sympathy with them. I do not say this to try to influence the minister because I have no idea that I would in-

fluence him. He apparently has fixed on a decided policy. If that is his policy, I would like him to make an announcement, do not do it in a concealed way, do not try to keep away from the point by saying: Oh look at Toronto, and make Toronto a scapegoat for everything. Toronto is a big city, but it is not the whole country and there are other parts of the community just as much entitled to consideration as Toronto.

I am sure that on reflection my hon. friend will not feel he has been very happy in his address to the committee. When I mentioned Toronto, I did it in good faith, simply to show that we are not generous to Toronto, but that we are just, as we are seeking to be just to all narts of the country. We cannot erect all the public buildings required at once, nor improve all the harbours. My hon. friend will recognize that I did not allow the fact that his constituency sends a Conservative to this parliament to interfere with my doing justice to the port of Oakville. I have made provision for improving that port. I would not allow the fact that my bon. friend represents that constituency to influence me. The hon. friend speaks of Toronto, and says that we are making a strong bid to win some seats in Toronto by erecting public buildings. If we had a vote here for a public building in the constituency of my hon. friend, he would say to his electors:	The Minister
of Public WoTks is trying to capture you by holding out >a bribe to you, and are you, the independent electors of Halton, not going to resent such an attempt as that to bribe you by the erection of a public building? It was not a happy speech of my hon. friend, and I am surprised that he should so forget himself as to depart from his ordinary practice of speaking with judgment.

I have heretofore taken the other stand. I have said to my people that I did not believe this government was corrupt enough to do that sort of thing and would only erect public buildings in ridings represented toy Liberals. But, I am sorry to say I have lost my good opinion of the Minister of Public Works to-night, notwithstanding, that he has given us a very respectable grant for the harbour at Oakville, which I think was generous and just. Oakville was entitled to it, Oakville has never had a public building and it is a very small sum, yet I feel thankful the minister did that, because if is an important port. It is a sort of harbour of refuge between Toronto and Hamilton, where boats can call and in the event of a storm can go in and ride at anchor in the harbour and be protected. Heretofore, I have defended the minister as I have said, and I am sorry that I had to-night to change my mind on that question.
Portage la Prairie public building-revote, $50,000.
When was the first amount put in the estimates for this building?
At the session of 1907-8.
Immediately before the election?
The election happened to take place afterwards. This is urgently asked for toy the people of Portage la Prairie.

Has the minister given any further consideration to the erection of a public building in the town of Carman, in the constituency I have the honour of representing? I have brought this to the attention of the Public Works Department every year since I have had the pleasure of sitting in this House. Carman is a town of over 2,000 inhabitants. It is a progressive little town, the citizens have expended a large amount of money in putting in a sewage system and water works, and if there is a town in Manitoba entitled to a public building, Carman is. The minister on former occasions, agreed that I had a good case, and said he would look into it and would undoubtedly give it the consideration to which it is entitled. Taking the minister at his word, I now have to say that if he has looked into it he certainly will have to come to that view and greet a building. Carman is a railway centre. Three lines of railway run through it, the Canadian Northern, the Canadian Pacific railway and the Great Northern, and I was in hopes that the minister would have placed in his estimates, an appropriation towards the construction of a customs office and post office there. Other towns throughout the Dominion which are much inferior to this have been given consideration. The postal revenue is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $5,000 a year, and the amount of business that goes through the post office is greater by 50 or 75 per cent than that of a large portion of the towns which have got public buildings. I bring it to the attention of the minister, and I hope that he will, before this House rises, see fit to put an appropriation in the supplementaries towards the construction of a public building in the town of Carman.

There are a great many places, without speaking particularly, where, I think, public buildings might be erected without exciting any just criticism. I do not say that they would not excite criticism, because my experience has been that no matter what care we exercise there will be some criticism. But, I have been obliged to omit them from the estimates. The supplementary estimates have been brought down, I do not anticipate that

there will be any more during the present session, and therefore, I am unable to give my hon. friend the assurance that he would like to have.
You might give us a promise and probably we will live on that for a year if you cannot go any further.
That is what I am not able to do.
Will the minister look into the case I have cited before the end of the session of parliament?
I have already looked into it.
Do you not think it is entitled to the consideration I have asked?

I can say to my hon. friend that if I had decided to have _a public building at Carman I would not expect that I could be very justly criticised for providing for it. But, outside of what my hon. friend has said, I have not had it urged upon my attention very strongly from the people. I have had no intimation from the Post Office Department that the people are suffering any particular inconvenience at Carman. But, I may say to my hon. friend that I will continue to give the matter consideration.

The minister has said that he has had no pressure brought upon him by the citizens of Carman. I might call his attention to several resolutions that, if he will take the trouble to look at the records, he will find either in his department or the Customs Department, passed by the board of trade and other organizations of Carman, and I might go a little farther, and say that I think he has strong letters from the citizens of Carman who are of the same political faith as he is. When he says that he had no representations from the city of Carman, if he will take the trouble to look at the records, he will find that what I have said is correct.
I will have the matter inquired into.
I suppose the Minister of Public Works is perfectly willing to say that he does not refuse to put a public building in a town, because it is represented by a Conservative!
I did not intend to make any such statement.

I think perhaps the minister would state that that would not be a guiding feature in his policy, that he does not decide where a public building shall be located by the character of its representation. What dojs he say in respect to that?
I always feel it to be my duty to give very careful consideration to the representations of our friends.
That hardly answers my question.
I think so.
I want the minister to say whether or not the fact that a county is represented by a Conservative is to be taken as a reason why a public building should not be erected.
No, these estimates prove the contrary to that.
These estimates prove that where a county is represented by a Liberal public money is expended,
And where represented by a Conservative, if a building is needed in the public interest, provision is made for it.
Just as freely?
In quite a number of cases.
Will the minister say just as freely?
Well that is a pretty hard question to put to me.
I will be perfectly satisfied if the minister will say so.
We would hear of it from the county of Halton.

I might further say that the citizens of Carman have been put to a great deal of inconvenience. Dutiable goods have been coming in there, and the fact that there is no port of entry has made it very inconvenient. The minister will find a requisition along those lines for a public building if he will look at the records.
That will be in the Customs Department.

Carman is one of the oldest towns in Manitoba. It is the first town that was established south of the As-siniboine river, and I state again that if there is a town in that province that is deserving of consideration at the hands of this government it is Carman.
Winnipeg examining warehouse (new), $25,000.
Will that complete?
Yes, it will complete the building.
Is this on Main street?
This is to fit up the post office building for savings bank and customs purposes.
Is $50,000 the entire cost of the alterations?

We expect that will complete The alterations.
Winnipeg immigration buildings-government's share of cost of asphalt pavement laid by municipal corporation on Maple street, between Higgins' Avenue and C. P. Ry., in front of buildings Nos. 1 and 5, $871.28.

The city collector of taxes sent me several communications about the pavement in front of several other public buildings in Winnipeg. I left these papers with the proper officer in your department, and I would request that the matters be expedited.

Pursuant to my direction the matter has been taken up by the proper officer in my department, and he is now in communication with the authorities of the city of Winnipeg on the subject.
Estevan-public building, $15,000.
What will be the total cost?

About $36,000. Estevan is quite an important and growing town, and the cost of building is greater there than in the east. We have to build for the future, perhaps more so than in the small towns in the east, because of the rapid growth.
I do not like to trouble the minister, but I tried to be here at eight o'clock and missed it. On the item for Uxbridge, Ontario, does the minister object to give me a little information about that?

No objection at all. We propose erecting a public building there, the cost of which will run to about $15,000. We expect to call for tenders during the present season as soon as plans and specifications can be prepared.
Is there a proposition before the minister in reference to having an armoury in the basement of the building?
Yes. There has been a suggestion made that there should be an armoury in a portion of the building. That, of course, will increase the cost, probably about $3,000.

I would like to urge that upon the minister. Uxbridge is quite a market town, and a good sized town. It is the headquarters of Company 5 of the 24th Regiment, and for a number of years,
as captain of that company, I have paid out of my own pocket the rental of an armoury. The young man who is in charge mow is a mechanic amd he cannot afford to pay the rental, I could not afford to pay it, but I did. I do not think it is fair, where a public building is being erected, for the government to ask the ' officers ' to pay for the rent of an armoury when it could be constructed in conjunction with this building. I think the idea would meet with the approval of the citizens. I would urge upon the minister that when they are drawing the plans they should draw them with the idea of having an armoury in the basement of the post office.
The matter will be noted, and carefully considered.
Then I would like to ask the minister if there were any objections taken to the site which has been selected?
The site has been purchased.
Were there any resolutions or petitions sent in to the minister objecting to it?
I do not at this moment recall any.
Upon whose recommendation was the site purchased?

We sent an inspector from the department to look over the different sites that were available, and it was upon his recommendation that this site was chosen. The price is very reasonable, $1,200. The property is a corner lot, 60 feet on one street by 90 on the other.

I understand that the majority of the citizens Object to the present site because it is not central enough, it is off at one end of the town. The central'site is the O'Neill site that the department had an option^ upon. What is the price of the O'Neill site?
I have not a memorandum of that. But the gentleman whom we sent there is <an expert in the business of selecting sites.
Did he receive any recommendations from public bodies?
I cannot tell my hon. friend, but if he desires I will have the matter looked up to-morrow and let him know.
Did he receive any legal expenses?
$52.74 for the legal expenses, including the travelling expenses of the inspector.
Have you the expense? separate?
I could not say as to that.
Was it Mr. Ormiston?
I have not any memorandum of that.
He got $49.45.

Would there be any chance of the minister changing the site? I understand that sometimes when citizens object to the site purchased the department make a change. The overwhelming sentiment of the town is that the central site at the market building should have been selected by the government. Three part? of the population reside in that part of the town, and if the central site had been selected it would have met with the unanimous approval of the citizens. I_was wondering if the department had any petitions or objections registered against this site?

I am satisfied that the site selected is a good one. I think it would be very objectionable now to attempt to make a change in the site; it would mean selling this piece of land, and it would mean dividing the people on the question of the site, which is always unfortunate. The site has been bought; it had better go on the present site.
I thought perhaps the department in selecting the site might have consulted the representative of the constituency, and the residents of the town.
No doubt the inspector consulted the people of the town; that is his duty, and those were his instructions.
Surely my hon. friend did not select the site in the town of Uxbridge without consulting the member for the county?
Yes, the sitting member was consulted.
What was his answer?
I do not know, but I know he was consulted.
What sitting member, may I ask?
Mr. Grant.
When wa3 the site purchased?
It was purchased in 1909; it was decided upon before that, in 1908.

About what date was it decided on?
Mr. PTTGSLEY
Some time in the summer of 1908, I think.

I think the minister is in error about the time of deciding upon the site. On the eve of the election there were three or four options taken on various sites, the options were allowed to expire, and after the election they took up this lot again. So it was not decided until after the election in 1908.

I do not know as to that. I can say that the gentleman who selected it is a man who would consult with the people, he would examine different sites, and he would give his judgment, as I have no doubt he did in this case. He is a man of very excellent judgment, and is not influenced by personal considerations at all.
Were there any public bodies sending in requisitions for this building, or did the Post Office Department ask for a new building?

There was a public meeting in the town as early as December, 1907, and they passed a resolution, and a memorial was sent in urging that a public building should be erected for a great many reasons, which are set forth in the memorial.
Would m,y hon. friend read that memorial?

It would take too long. I will send it over to my hon. friend.
Lethbridge immigration building-removal of building to new site, and repairs, renewals, etc., $6,000.
This requires some explanation. We want to know why the building was removed, and how far it has been removed. .'This is a considerable' amount for removing a building of an ordinary size.

The cost of the site was $2,200; and the estimated cost of moving the building to the new site, and repairing the same, and putting it in a state of completion, as per tender of Smith Brothers and Wilson, is $3,650; contingencies, $150, making a total of $6,000.
How far was it moved, and why was it moved?

It was because the Interior Department urged that it should be moved. In these western cities, which are growing, some of them with great rapidity, it becomes necessary sometimes to move the buildings to more convenient situations or for other reasons. In this particular case, I believe the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, who ovraed the land and leased it to the department.

wanted it, and it became necessary to move this building to another lot.
I am sorry you are so poor in a country where you own so much land
It is to be regretted

Has the minister had any representations from the Post Office Department regarding a public building in the town of Macleod? I have had very serious complaints from there in regard to the post office, which is certainly not suitable to the place. The Postma'ster General has spoken to me several times on the subject, and has said that he hoped that something would be done in the near future.

I may say that quite recently, and only quite recently, I did receive a representation from the people of Macleod, urging that a public building should be erected, but it was too late to take the matter up during the present session.
Is it under serious consideration for next year, and may the people hope that it will be erected then?
There are degrees of consideration.

The town is a very important one, with <a population of nearly 2,500, and with two railways. The mail is distributed in a small room about six feet by ten feet, and the condition is most serious. The place is not at all suitable for a post office in a town of its importance. It is a disgrace to the department.

I may say to my hon. friend that I have directed that a report be obtained from the Post Office Department as to the condition of affairs at Macleod with the view of giving the matter my serious consideration between now and the next session of parliament.
Strathcona immigration building-improvements, $3,000.
Apparently Strath-cona is rather a doubtful constituency.
That is not a kindly remark to make. There are also three items for Lethbridge.
This is a pretty large item for repairs. Will the minister give us some idea of what it is for?

The building was constructed in 1900. It is a wooden building, set up on wooden posts, and these improvements are all absolutely required. The building has cost in the way of construction up to the 31st March, i909, $7,407.08. and there have been repairs to the amount of $1,548.35. The building is 2J stories,
55 feet by 28 feet, and there is a 3-story annex in the rear, 32 feet by 10 feet. It contains kitchen, baggage room, dormitories, washroom and storeroom.
Are these immigration buildings finished on the inside with boards or plastered??
This is plastered.

May I ask the minister if he will supply at the next sitting of the committee a list of the newspapers, with the amount paid to each, in which advertisements were inserted for tenders for public buildings at Whitby to the amount of $354.95, at Welland to the amount of $340.80, at Leamington to the amount of $362.94, and at Dauphin, Man., to the amount of $236.91.

I will be glad to do that.
Chilliwack, B.C., public building, $10,000.
Will the minister kindly tell the committee what his intentions are in regard to this building?

The intention is to purchase a site and later on to proceed with the erection of a public building. I may say we have not yet purchased the site.
I believe there is a considerable difference of opinion as to what would be a proper site for the building. We have made a good deal of inquiry and have had our good deal of inquiry and have had our representative there, but we intend to completing the purchase. Perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor), who is familiar with the situation, would let me know what he thinks of the present post office site, for the new building.

That is rather a delicate question to ask because I happen to have possession of the adjoining property. I would like to say, however, that Chilliwack is really suffering very much for the want of this building. I do not think there is any place in the whole country where one is needed more.
Feruie public building-$10,000.
This is to complete the public building at Fernie.

Is that a post office
building?
Yes, that is a post office building now under contract.

I have a long letter
here a column and a half in length, the writer of which states that he has had to wait as long as half an hour and three-quarters of an hour in order to register a letter owing to the bad accommodation there.
In the new building?
That is what I wanted to know.

That would be in the old building. The letter shows the necessity for the new building, which is nearly completed.
Greenwood public building-revote of $5,000, lapsed, $10,000.
Mx\ PLAIN. Wlia^t will this builtling cost?
I do not think we can get this constructed for less than $25,000 to $30,000. Greenwood is quite an important place.
When was the item first put in the estimates?

I think it was put in the estimates in 1908-9, but I am not sure. However, Ithink there is no question about the building being very urgently required, and I regret that I have not been able to build it before this.
Vancouver public building-$15,000.
Is that the post office building?

The new post office.
Williamshead quarantine station-improvements and repairs to building and fittings, etc., $5,000.
Before we pass from the British Colombia items, will all this work in British Columbia be done after public tenders have been invited?

Yes, unless some repairs, but all the new buildings will be constructed after public advertisement and tenders.
General-tobacco curing experimental stations, $5,000.
What are these?
These are requested by the Department of Agriculture.
Where are these stations to be located?	[DOT]

The intention, as I understood, is to put one in Ontario and one in Quebec.
Ottawa public buildings-grounds, $12,000.
Wha t grounds are these?
These are the parliamentary grounds.
There is a contract, I understand.
No, it is all done by day work under our own foreman.
Do you mean to say that it costs $12,000 a year to keep up the parliamentary grounds?
Yes.
And they are very badly kept at that.
Do they include the grounds at Rideau Hall?
This item does not include the grounds at Rideau Hall.
Walking around the rear of this building to-day I found the cedar hedge in very bad order. It ought to be replaced. Perhaps the minister has not noticed it.

I notice that it is unsightly. But, if it were taken away, we should be under the necessity of putting up a nice substantial fence which would be expensive, and so we have not decided to do anything iyet.
Why not replant the hedge?-it would be much handsomer than a fence.
It might not be a success. My hon. friend (Mr. Goodeve) knows that here as elsewhere, cedar hedges have not been thriving of recent years.

All the trees around the summer house and the Queen's statue have been allowed to die for want of throwing a little water on them. I think that the grounds receive very poor attention. I would invite the minister, the first time he goes to Toronto, to observe the way the parliament grounds there are looked after. It seems to me that the men in charge here are not competent to do the work. The condition is simply disgraceful.

We are supposed to have, and I believe we have, a first-class foreman gardener. I will see that my hon. friend's views are conveyed to him.
Rideau Hall, including grounds, improvements, furniture and maintenance, $35,000.

This item ought to be explained. When our friends who now occupy the treasury benches were in opposition, they used to find a great deal of fault with a much smaller expenditure on Rideau Hall than this. And perhaps the minister could tell us what becomes of the old furniture that is put out of the building. Every year, there seems to be a lot of new furniture purchased, but I have never been able to find what was done with the old. It would be good enough, I fancy, for the houses of most of us. But these things seem to be appropriated by some one and no account given.
My hon. friend is entirely in error. All the old furniture which seems to be of no use is auctioned off and the proceeds go into the treasury.
Perhaps the minister would give us an account of that.
I cannot give it tonight, but if my hon. friend would like it I will have it prepared.
I would like to have it.
I have asked the chief architect to make a note of it.
Now, perhaps the minister would tell us how this money is expended.

The best way would be to give some details of the expenditure of the past year:	decorating dining room,
$1,600; tennis court, $720; plants, bulbs and seeds, $992; dry goods, &c., $6,533; lumber, $1,752; hardware, paint and glass, $1,376; furniture, flags, cleaning carpets, &c., $1,231; sand, cement and manure, $305; salaries, &c., $18,110; sundries, $180. That is the expenditure up to December, and gives my hon. friend an idea of how the money goes.
When I get the other account I shall have made a start for what I am after. I have a lot of figures, and I think they come to a good deal more than the minister has given.

I will get the information my hon. friend (Mr. U. Wilson) wants.
Dominion cattle quarantine stations, renewals, repairs, &c., $20,000.
Mr. iPUGSLEY. In this case, as in others, 25 per cent of the amount has already been voted. And as the amount voted, $5,000, is sufficient, I move that this item be struck out.
How does this happen?'
We find that under this head we do not require more than $5,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Item struck cut.
Yukon public buildings, rents, repairs, fuel, light, water services and caretakers' salaries, $60,000.
How is the money for Yukon public buildings to be expended?

It will be the same as last year, rent, repairs and renewals, light, fuel, caretakers' salaries, etc. I am asking the same vote as last year, and I have no doubt my hon. friend will find in the Auditor General's Report a full statement.
Interior Department, civil government- salaries, $876,866.27.	/
There seems to be a large increase?

I notice the number of officials in the Interior Department is to be increased from 670 up to 722. Is the minister simply making provision for that increased number, or are they already at work in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Owing to the increase of work in the department we were compelled to employ a larger number of temporary clerks during the last year than we had provision for in the estimates. They were employed under the Act, and were paid out of the contingencies vote. I desire now to provide for that number in the permanent vote, and that accounts for the larger part of this increase. These people have been in employment under the Civil| Service Act as temporaries. We wish to make permanent provision for them, and also for further requirements to meet the increase of work. We would prefer to emi ploy permanent people, because the employment of temporaries is not satisfactory. Under the Civil Service Act we cannot employ a temporary clerk for more than four months in any one year, and of course where we have permanent work that is most unsatisfactory no matter how efficient the clerks may be.
How many temporary clerks were employed last year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: About forty-five.
You are providing for fifty-two new ones this year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Forty-five were in employment temporarily. We are making provision for fifty-two, including forty-five permanents instead of these forty-five temporaries, and as our work increases we will be able to take on further permanents up to the total number of fifty-two.
Do the temporaries have to pass the Civil Service examination?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Under the Act we cannot employ any one who has not passed the Civil Service examination and been approved by the commission.
Why do they have to go in four months?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Because the Civil Service Act says they can only be employed for four months.
Contingencies, $47,600.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The increase of $10,000 in contingencies is due to an increase in the amount of printing and stationery, owing to the increased business of the department by reason of the larger number . of homestead entries with consequent-issue of patents, etc.
Is any of this printing done outside of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not of this vote; this is all done in the Printing Bureau.
Immigration-salaries of agents and employees in Canada, Great Britain and foreign countries, $200,000.
I think this requires some explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The amount is the same as was voted last year, and the division is as follows:	Salaries in Canada, $117,-
412; United States, $42,180; Great Britain and Ireland, $34,834; Europe, $5,500.
Where have you W. T. R. Preston now?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Preston is in the Department of Trade and Commerce. He has not been in the Interior Department for some years.

I want to call the attention of the minister to the fact that we have had an inspector on the Bay of Quinte railway. I put a question on the paper the other day asking how many immigrants had been located along that line. The answer was that they did not keep track of those located, and I do not know what they want an inspector there for. They also gave the information that they had deported sixty-eight. Following that question I asked how many had been located between Deseronto and a place just at the other side of Tweed-I forgot the name. I find that the department are in the habit of sending their special agents to the old country every year. Has that been done this year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
And that they employ some of them the year round?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, some of the men who are in employment the year round are sent to Great Britain during the season of immigration effort.
Have you not some who are not employed the year round that you send abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I find there is Anson Aylesworth, and I do not want to make any exception in his case, because he happens to be a brother of a minister. The only exception I take is that I think this officer was entirely unnecessary. He was immigration agent in the old country, and the Auditor General's Report for 1908 shows that it cost this country $988.98 for a trip occupying four months which I call a pleasure trip. I moved two years ago for a return showing the reports that these people who went as special agents to the old country had made to the government. I did not find any reports made by any of these gentlemen. Mr. Walker, the assistant superintendent of immigration in London, made a report. He spoke in glowing terms of the success of these gentlemen, and told how they had eloquently addressed public meetings, how they had attracted jl great deal of attention, and he added that afterwards there had been a great many inquiries made as to this country. But, I did not find any particular report from him as to the number of people that they had induced to come to this country. At page K-118 of last year's Auditor General's Report Mr. Aylesworth is put down as superintendent of immigration on the Bay of Quinte railway. The report shows that he received $100 a month. The total cost to the country was $1,070.14. I would like to know what Mr. Aylesworth did as inspector on that road. I have no knowledge of any considerable number of immigrants being placed anywhere along that line except that they were sent to Deseronto during the time we had that great influx in 1907. The work gave out, some were deported, some returned to Napanee, some were scattered in various places, and they were a pretty unsuccessful lot of people. In addition to his other duties Mr. Aylesworth found it necessary to come to Napanee during the election and deliver an address in the committee room of the Liberal party. He did that at the last general election. At that time I did not know that he was in the government employ; I presumed that he had had his pleasure trip to the old country, and was through. But,
I found that he was constantly in'the employ of the government. I would like to know whether Mr. Aylesworth is still in the employ of the government as a regular official, what his salary is, and what his duties are? I do not take any exception to Mr. Aylesworth as an officer, but I think he should keep out of committee rooms, and refrain from making speeches. I remember that the right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) made a promise to this. House that any civil servant that dabbled in politics would be given an opportunity to devote all his. time to politics, but in those days most of the officials were Conservatives, and most likely a great many of them were dealt with accordingly, but I have never known of a single instance where he dismissed a Liberal for interfering in politics. There are some other matters that, I want to speak about, but I would like to hear what the minister has to say about Mr. Aylesworth, and his conduct in interfering in the elections, and what his duties were as inspector of the Bay of Quinte railway.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Aylesworth was em-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: .ployed temporarily-I cannot give just the time-as a farm delegate. He was a practical farmer.
The return says four months.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He was employed temporarily as a farm delegate in the old country. I think it is not necessary to enter into a disquisition as to the value of the services rendered by these farm delegates, but I think the results of their work in past years is very well shown In the quantity and character of the immigration we are getting this year. However, Mr. Ayles-worth was employed temporarily, and we believed that he gave satisfactory service. He afterwards was given employment as inspector of the farm labour distributing agencies that we have throughout Ontario. If he is listed in the Auditor General's Report simply as immigration inspector on the Bay of Quinte railway it is not a correct statement of his duties.
That is what it says.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not a correct statement of his duties, because his duties are not confined to the Bay of Quinte railway; in fact, I do not know that they have any particular connection with the Bay of Quinte railway. He is simply employed in Ontario inspecting the agencies which we have throughout the province to distribute farm labour, and during the season of immigration effort In the old country we have employed him during the past two years for three or four months. We believe that he is a very satisfactory officer. We have every reason to believe so; we thought he should be so by reason of his experience, character and ability. His salary when employed is $100 a month. I have no knowledge of the part he took in the election. If he was in the employ of the department I certainly think he should not have taken that part. I care not who he is, if he is drawing government money to an amount sufficient for his livelihood, if that is his salary, he should certainly have given his whole time to the government, and should not have interfered in elections. But I am not at this moment aware whether he was in permanent employment of the government at the time. Of course if he "was not in permanent .employment, the position is somewhat different.

I do not take any particular objection to Mr. Aylesworth speaking against me in that election. He stumped against me in 1892, and our fellows rather made sport of him, pretending to speak for the other man while he was talking in my favour. He is a glib tongued chap, quite a good speaker. In
the Auditor General's Report for 1908, vol. 2, I find these items:
K-30 G. A. Aylesworth as special agent to England four months to 31st March at $100 per month, railway fares, $88.40; travelling expenses, $400.58, total $988.98. Return February 4, 1910.
5-G. A. Aylesworth January, 1909, for four months got $833.24. Auditor General's Report, 1909.
K-118 G. A. Aylesworth as inspector on the Bay of Quinte for nine months, $1,070.14.
I hardly know where he got his Pullmans on the Bay of Quinte railway. I never heard of Pullmans on that railway. I just call the attention of the minister to this item, because it looks to me absurd for any man who is inspector of immigration on a little railway like the Bay of Quinte. I recollect talking to the station agent, who was distribution agent of immigration at Yarker during the election. He had been appointed as one of the men to locate immigrants, and he said, I never located any. But you remember a man by the name of Miller, and he stole some money from the government that he had to refund, but the government never made him come to time as they would an ordinary criminal. If an ordinary man had settled with a criminal as they did with Miller, it seems to me he would have got into trouble. I would like some explanation about the children that Children's Aid Societies are bringing to this country, whether they pass a regular examination like ordinary immigrants; also I would like some information about grants to the different women's societies that bring out females, and I would like to know whether they also have to pass examination like ordinary immigrants. Then would the minister say whether female domestics are examined like ordinary immigrants. I see bonuses were paid on them to the amount of $4,878. I would like an explanation of the different societies to which you give bonuses, and whether all these people have to pass an examination like ordinary immigrants. I suppose you have got a number of inspectors, and I hope they are more useful than out friend Aylesworth has been, apparently. Tell us how many inspectors you have, where they are located, and what their duties are. I suppose they report to the department from time to time. There was another matter that I used to be interested in before the Agriculture Committee, that is, as to what reports were made by agents who were getting salaries. I have not heard of any of them reporting the numbers they sent in. But we always get reports from the men on commission, and I wondered sometimes whether they worked together. It seems strange that we never heard any particulars about the men on salaries sending in great numbers of people. But they do come in here in large

droves, and we find in the Public Accounts considerable bonuses paid for them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In regard to the children who are brought out, they, as well as all other immigrants have to pass a medical inspection at the port of landing. There is no exception in that respect. But the children who are brought out are also subject to medical inspection before they leave the old country, that is, they are required to have a medical certificate before they start, but that does not relieve them from the medical inspection on their arrival in Canada. The same is true in regard to all people who land in Canada as immigrants, whether brought out by societies or not. We have inspectors for various purposes in different branches of the immigration 'service. We have one inspector whose duty it is to look after distributing agents, that is, those who are authorized to secure employment for farm labourers throughout Ontario. Mr. Ayles-worth is the only inspector we have for that purpose. Then we have inspectors for the boundary inspection service, or the exclusion service, as it might be called. We have inspectors also of the children who are placed in homes throughout the country. So we have three different classes of inspectors. But we have only one inspector for the farm labour distributing agents.
Does that inspector report to you?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Where is that report t) be found?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Those reports are in the department, they can be produced on an order of the House. They are not printed; if we printed all the reports we get they would make a very bulky volume, and probablv not be required. But the reports are in the department and can be produced.
Does Mr. Aylesworth travel on a pass?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, he has a pass.
Over all the roads?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All the large railway1, svstems. The societies whose names are mentioned on page 124 of the Auditor General's Report for 1908-09, simply get the ordinary bonus on the people they bring out, under the regulations, the same as any other agents. They do not receive any special consideration. They get $5 a head on domestic servants, but not on factory women or any other kind.

What guarantee have you that these are domestic servants who come to this country? I see that the On-Mr. U. WILSON.'
tario government are also giving a bonus on domestic servants. I do not approve of it, but they insist that a domestic servant must bring a letter from a clergyman as to her standing, and a recommendation from her last employer in this country, 'before the agent gets the $5. So far as I know, with this government all one has to do is to pass as a domestic servant and the agent gets the $5. Is that the case?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. The agent who claims the bonus has to tell us where the person on whom the bonus is claimed is employed. We then inquire of the employer, and on receiving a satisfactory reply, we pay the bonus.
How do you apply- by letter?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. It might interest my hon. friend to know that in the immigration branch last year we got 220,000 letters.
Were they all answered?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All that required answer.

I am informed that about at present 100 domestics are , expected to arrive in Toronto, in two parties of, I think, 50 each. Does the minister know anything of that or whether they are brought out under Dominion or provincial arrangement?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no specific knowledge of any party of that particular number. As my hon. friend is aware, the Ontario government is at present taking an active interest in immigration work, and it might be a party they were taking a special interest in. I may say that, as a department, we do not specially undertake to bring out domestic servants or to assume responsibility in regard to them. They are taken in hand by parties who make practically a business of conveying them out and seeing to the placing of them. We recognize the people who do this as long as we think they do it satisfactorily, and they get the benefit of the bonus.

Of course, I do not agree with that view, because I think people who want servants ought to pay for them. When your inspectors are away from your office, I suppcrse you pay their board and lodging and their fare?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Mr. Aylesworth could not have been away a great deal, because I find that hi3 board and lodging cost only $116.50, whereas the board and lodging of Mr. Mclnnis, of Detroit, cost $513. Mr. Aylesworth paid only $3.75 for sleeping car, $19.04 for transfer of baggage, and

$11.40 for fares. I understood that Mr. Mclnnis was supposed to be located in Detroit. Either one of two things have happened: either Mr. Aylesworth has not travelled a great deal as the general agent of the department to locate farmers throughout Ontario, or Mr. Mclnnis got a good board for very little travelling, or lived pretty well for a man supposed to be living in Detroit.

It is rather a mistake to suppose that the agent in Detroit has no other duty than to attend to the office there, The business of Mr. Mclnnis, as of all our agents of that class in the United States, is to go wherever in the state it may seem to him to be necessary to go, either to hold meetings, to give information, or to assist prospective settlers in commencing their journey.
Have you not several agents in that state?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. The only office we have is in Detroit, and Mr. Mclnnis is the agent. While he has control of the office, his business is more important outside of the office than in the office. Mr. Aylesworth has not the same class of duty at all. His business is simply to visit the different men who are authorized to act as distributors of farm labour, and it may easily be seen that such duties do not require nearly as heavy expenses as the duties of Mr. Mclnnis.

I think Mr. Mclnnis' office cost more than $8,000 a year. Although it is a rented building, he put a stone front on it and plate glass windows in it. Why should he put on such expensive repairs instead of the owner of the property? If the owner wants to rent the building, he ought to put it in a rentable shape. I think Mr. Mclnnis pays $900 a year for rent.
