speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: And he does his own repairs. Is it pretty general in your department to allow your agents to rent buildings at such prices, as they like, and then to make such repairs as they think fit at the public expense of Canada, instead of renting a suitable building and letting the landlord do the repairs? That is done in several cases, and I think it should not be continued.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will take all the responsibility upon myself for the expense of fitting up the office at Detroit. Some years ago when I first visited Detroit, our office was in an upper room, where a visitor under ordinary circumstances would not find it, although it was in a very good street, and it seemed to me that if we were trying to do business in an agricultural 260
state like Michigan, and in a city like Detroit, which is the centre of an agricultural population, it was not economy to have an office in an upper room not convenient to the public or in the public view. Other people who are trying to attract public attention, who are trying to do business with the public, obtain the best situation and make the best front they can, and I took the responsibility of authorizing our inspector for the United States, Mr. William White, to secure a building or office accommodation that would be better adapted to our purposes, and the accommodation was secured. We made the best arrangement we could as to rental, and we would have had to pay more rental if we had not put in the fittings ourselves. We wanted the fittings to suit our purposes, and I think it will be agreed by those who have seen our office that we have a very suitable place for the purposes we have in view, and one entirely creditable to our country. I do not think it is economy to spend $8,000 in rent and salaries for an office, the purpose of which is to get in touch with the public, and not get full value for the sake of spending a few hundred dollars more in order to secure a good situation and an office with a good appearance and proper conveniences and appliances.

I am very sorry that, there was not another building in Detroit that was suitable and that might havie< been rented without a great deal of expense on repairs. That is a very exceptional situation in any city or town, for you can easily get a suitable place without putting on repairs. So far as my knowledge goes a landlord who has his' rent assured would prefer to meet the tenant on reasonable terms. The fact that the minister takes the full responsibility does not alter the case a bit. He might have done what he thought was best, but, that is a matter of opinion. I think he should not have required so many repairs.

Before we leave this item I wish to draw the attention of the minister and the House to a matter I previously discussed and to offer an explanation of some statements I made in this House on the 22nd March of this year, when a similar item was undier consideration. On that occasion I called the attention of the minister to a statement that was alleged to have been made by Bruce Walker who, I thought at that time, was Commissioner of Immigration for the Dominion in all foreign countries, but who, I now understand, is Commissioner of Immigration to the United States. I find that the remarks I then made have been very much misinterpreted or misquoted. The newspapers in my locality, thp southern part of Alberta, have construed my re-

There are supplementary estimates for this service of $125.000, making an aggregate appropriation of $1,040,000, which is the highest estimate we have ever had for immigration up to this date, I believe. What has occurred since the main estimates were prepared to make it necessary to have this supplementary vote?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is partly due to the greater precautions being taken from time to time in the exclusion of undesirables, and partly to the very great increase in the number of immigrants coming this year for whom we have to provide. The main estimates were prepared in the fall of last year. We could not know then what the movement this year would be. The hon. gentleman (Mr. U. Wilson) knows that the movement this year is beyond all previous records.

Is there any record of what these agencies do? For instance, the Detroit agency is an expensive one. Un-

less it pays by the number of immigrants it is not desirable to keep it going. I think a record should be kept of what the agencies do, to ascertain whether they pay or not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is not possible for us to keep a record of the results of the work of any agent or agency, for the reason that we have no control over the movement of people. We can only judge of the results of the work of the agency by the movement from the locality it serves. My hon. friend (Mr. Beattie) is aware that the movement of people from the United States during the past few years has been increasing, and is particularly large this year. We do not claim all the credit for that for our agents, but we do claim that they are a contributing cause, and that the continual growth of the movement is evident that good work is done. I have not the figures before me, but I think the record of the homestead entries from the different states will show that there is good work done in the state of Michigan by the agency there.
Do the agents give a monthly, or a yearly report?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A monthly report. There is also the annual report which appears in the blue-book, but it would be too cumbrous to publish their monthly reports.
How much did you spend last year in the aggregate?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have not the full accounts for the last year, but I am informed that the total expenditure, including that from the supplementary estimates for the year, will amount to about $975,000. In the year 1908-9, the Auditor General's Report shows an expenditure of $979,326.
If you add the supplementaries for last year $60,000, you will have an expenditure of over $1,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The estimates I have given includes the expenditures from the supplementaries. Including this, the expenditure will be about $975,000.

Speaking of Mr. Ayles-worth, the minister said he was travelling on a pass, which accounted for his not charging so much for railway fares. How many of the agents of the Immigration Department make use of passes, and how are these passes paid for if at all?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Is not the minister aware that the granting of these passes is illegal under the Railway Act. It is legislated against in this country as discrimination. Under the Railway Act, there are certain passes that may be issued, but such passes as the minister refers to are not ampng them. When travelling on trains, I have observed these officials with passes. I thought perhaps they were travelling on private business; but it was no affair of mine, and I am not a detective. But, if these passes are gratuitous, if they are not paid for by the government in some way, they are contrary to the Railway Act of this country.
My object in asking was to find whether these passes were paid for, and so would form an addition to the expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have all the burden I can carry in administering the immigration law, and the land law, without administering the Railway Act.
How many officials of the Immigration Department^ such as doctors, are there at Halifax, and what are their salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This vote. covers the salaries of the medical officers. There are two medical officers at Halifax, Dr. Hawkins and Dr. Chisholm, and their salaries are $1,800 each.
Has any one been acting there besides these two doctors?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Dr. Chisholm broke his arm some time ago and another doctor has been acting in bis place.

What do you pay him
for his services?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He was paid $150 a month for the time he was employed.
Dr. Chisholm was paid his full salary, and Dr. Hogan, who was acting in his place would get $150 a month?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is right.
Are you awaTe that Dr. Hogan is also military doctor there and has a private practice as well?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no knowledge of that.
Are these doctors permitted to have a private practice?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, there is no restriction on them in that particular.

It seems rather unfair that medical men should be paid from $1,800 to $4,000 by the government, and should at the same time carry on a private practice in competition with other medical men who are not receiving such salaries.

In Halifax, I understand, there are eight or ten medical men thus employed. It would seem to me to be more fair in cities to make one medical man the government doctor and pay him a sufficient salary to enable him to live without carrying on a private practice in competition with other medical men. This is a matter that the government should look into.
Immigration-Contingencies, in Canadian, British, foreign agencies and general immigration expenses, $700,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is the same amount as last year.
Is any provision made in Canadian cities for looking after immigrants after they arrive? Is there any such provision in Toronto?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In some cities there is provision and in others not. We have provision at the ports of landing, St. John, Halifax and Quebec. We have detention accommodation in Montreal and general accommodation in Winnipeg and various other distributing points throughout the western country. We have none at Toronto. We have an information office there but no accommodation for immigrants.

I believe that Toronto is quite an important distributing point. Most of the farmers go there to get their help, and I have noticed lately something in the paper about the British Welcome League and their work. There is no doubt they are doing good work, and if it were not for such an institution there would sometimes be great hardship in Toronto. Would the minister not look into this matter and see if it would not be advisable to establish some sort of a place at Toronto where immigrants could be taken charge of while waiting to be taken up. Years ago there was an immigration shed where people went to pick out their help and I think it would be well to have a shelter where they could at least have a bed and be kept from the streets. It is not fair to rely on the Welcome League to do all this kind of work.

I notice a newspaper report of trouble between the agent of the British Immigration League at Winnipeg and the Immigration Department-. Has the minister received any communication with reference to that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I saw that item and communicated with the commissioner at Winnipeg and have his side of the case. 1 should be glad to give it to the House in a minute.
In regard to Toronto, many years ago, under the system of immigration effort that then prevailed, there was aocommo-Mr. CROSBY.
dation for immigrants at Toronto, Kingston, Hamilton and possibly other points in Ontario. After a time it was decided that the work of caring for immigrants in the province of Ontario might better be handled by the province than by the Dominion, and these different buildings which were used for the accommodation of immigrants were closed. Then for a number of years the Dominion made no provision and the province made such provision as was made. The province, I think, had some arrangements for caring for immigrants at Toronto. That did not seem to be satisfactory to the province, and after a while they abandoned it and gave the Dominion authorities notice that if they wanted to take any interest in immigration effort at Toronto, they were free to do so. Under the circumstances that had existed while the province had handled the matter at Toronto, using Toronto as a converging and distributing point, a sort of depot of immigrants, there seemed to have grown up a very considerable congestion of immigration at Toronto, and it seemed to us when we took fhe matter over that our business was rather to keep the immigrants out of Toronto than to get them in there, and we established throughout Ontario commission agents, whose business it was to find places for immigrants, placing an officer in Toronto to give information to immigrants that would carry them out of Toronto; that is to say to provide them with information which would enable them to make their railway connections in Toronto and generally secure and give out information that might be helpful, but in no way to make provision for the entertainment of the immigrants in Toronto, our business, as we understand it, being to keep the immigrant out of Toronto, to see that he gets on the farm and therefore we do not assist him in any way to stay in the city. That is the attitude that we have taken in regard to Toronto. As far as the matter has gone yet it has been more satisfactory than the former system. There is private effort for the entertainment of immigrants. There is the -Salvation Army and the Welcome League, both of which have accommodation. I think very probably that these institutions, both of which are very worthy in their way, meet the case as it is there to better advantage than if the government undertook it, because experience showed that it is in the interest of Toronto and in the interest of the province, that the immigrants should not be induced to congest in Toronto, but that they should be sent out to wherever their labour will yield the most advantage to themselves and the country as quickly as possible.

Around Toronto there is quite a farming district. In the townships of Scarboro and Markham and west of the

city quite a number of labourers are needed to work on the farms, and the farmers come to Toronto to get their help. Immigrants have to stay in Toronto for some little time before they are taken up, although in some cases they are snapped up as soon as they arrive, and the Welcome League have a lot to do, and have done a lot of good. If, on investigation, it is found that the British Welcome League are able to handle this work in a satisfactory manner I think it would be up to the government to help the league by giving them a grant each year. There is no doubt they have been doing good work, and the people of Toronto have had to put up for it, and they have done it willingly. I think it is only fair that these people who are working, not for the benefit of Toronto, but for the benefit of the outside country, should receive consideration.

There is considerable complaint from farmers that they find difficulty, notwithstanding the large influx of immigrants, in getting men. I had some letters during the present session about it saying that they had written to Toronto, and had written down here, and yet they had failed to get any satisfactory answer. They complain that while the country is paying out a lot of money for immigration, the immigrants are all shipped through to the west, and there is little opportunity for the farmers of Ontario, and the eastern provinces to get the help which is required. That seems to be one of the troubles. If you write down here they refer you to Toronto, but when you get to Toronto there does not appear to be very much chance of getting any satisfactory information as far as I can understand. Farmers complain that there is a disposition to send the immigrants to the prairie provinces, and not make any arrangement for a distribution through the older provinces as well.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We were able to place about 20,000 farm labourers in Ontario last year, but the demand is greater than the supply. We have no contract to do it, but we are not able to meet the demand when the demand is as large as it is. We have made a very reasonable effort. We have established these distributing agents throughout the country, and the distributing agent in the hon. gentleman's county would communicate directly with the booking agent in the old country.
There is a distributing agent at Flesherton, but he does not know anything about it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Our agent at Flesherton would make inquiry among the farmers of the surrounding country as to how many wanted labourers, and what wages they
would pay, and then he would communicate with the booking agents in the old country informing them that there were so many positions available in the vicinity of Flesherton in the expectation that the booking agent, knowing that these places were available, would be able to induce people to book direct to Flesherton.
What do these agents know about the booking agents or where to write?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are informed on the subject, and that is the way they are supposed to carry on their business. Our idea is to get as direct communication as possible between the farm and the immigrant, and by all means to avoid the direction of the immigrant to Toronto as his ultimate destination. Our whole idea is to direct him only through Toronto to his ultimate destination, and we have the office in Toronto for that purpose. We have an agent there for the purpose of giving information to immigrants, and for the purpose of giving information to farmers as well. The services of our agents are available to either the farmer or the immigrant, but we do not think, in the light of our former experience, that it is well for us to do anything in the way of entertainment at Toronto.
^-r- U- WILSON. Will the minister tell us what change he has made in the pay of the distributing agents? I think it has been greatly cut from what it used to be The amount used to be $2 per head for every man, woman and child in a family that went on a farm.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We pay now $2 for the farm labourer himself, but not for any member of his family unless it should be that his wife was going to domestic service, m which case the agent would get a commission on her employment also.

I would like to suggest to the minister Uiat in place of the distributing agents in the various towns writing to the booking agents in the old country, they should write to the head of the Immigration Department here. I believe that a great many of these agents throughout the country do not write as well as they should to the booking agents I think it would be better for them to write to the head of the Immigration Department and let the head of the Immigration Department distribute the immigrants according to his judgment.
I would like to ask the minister how far the territory of the agent extends east, west or north from Toronto?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He has no specific territory. His office is in Toronto. His business is to give information to the immi-

grants who are passing through as to their trains and destinations. His business also is to answer any inquiries that may come to him with regard to labourers. Any inquiry that comes to him from any part of the province it is his business to attend to as best he can. Wherever the farmer may come from, whether it is five, ten or a hundred miles away, it makes no difference; if Mr. Stewart is able to find a suitable person for him, of course, that man gets the benefit of it, and if he is not, there is no help for the situation.
Then the farmer in Markham would have to come to Toronto?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He could either come or write. Mr. Stewart said -to me: The man who comes in here naturally gets the preference. When the man is here and is able to see the man he wishes to engage, and when the man who wants the engagement is able to see the farmer, it is very much more satisfactory than communicating by letter. The man who comes to Toronto gets the advantage over the man who writes, but the man who writes gets the information as well as it can be given to him.

That goes to prove that there is need for some accommodation in Toronto for these immigrants. The farmer who leaves his work and comes in gets the best man,- and there is no doubt that the best time to select a man is when you can see him. It would be unsatisfactory to undertake to select a man who was away across the ocean with no means of knowing what kind of a man would be senit out. Farmers generally do not realize that they want a man until the very day they need him, and then they run to town and try to find a man. I think that the minister should give consideration to the question of providing better accommodation for immigrants in Toronto. Some years ago the number of immigrants conn ing to this country was a great deal less' than it is now. Everything has gone ahead so rapidly with the immigration business that it is getting almost beyond control. I think it would be wise to have something set aside to provide for accommodation for these people in Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In the light of experL ence it was our judgment that it was better not to provide accommodation in Toronto by the Dominion government. It is not for any lack of attention to the matter, or any lack of willingness to do it. But judging from our experience in 1906-7 when there was such a congestion of immigration in Toronto, we did not think it was desirable by offering accommodation there to favour that congestion. As I told the representatives of the Ontario government when they spoke to us about taking over Mr. OLIVER.
the office in Toronto, I said our business will be to keep the immigrants away from Toronto, not to bring them there, or entertain them there.

It is desirable that there should be some central place where people can go and get a man. Sometimes it is impossible for weeks or months to get such a man as you want. It frequently happens that a man is sent who turns out to be absolutely no good. For instance, a man was sent to me who couldn't even drive a horse. I set him digging post holes, and he spent the whole afternoon at one post hole. What is needed is some central place where the farmers can go and select such a man as will suit his. purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend asked me in regard to a matter that occurred in' Winnipeg, and which was mentioned in the papers. I inquired from the commissioner in Winnipeg, and he replied as fol-fows:
Man named Rogers, presumably local president English Welcome League, refused admission to immigration hall here late Monday night by night watchman acting upon my general instructions. Have hitherto refused to permit unknown and unauthorized young men access to the immigration halls under any pretext after 10 o'clock at night_ as in this particular case. If Rogers admission was desired or desirable it would doubtless have been arranged by the simple expedient of applying to the proper authority.

I would like to know from the minister on what class of immigrants the government pay bonuses. If it is domestic immigrants, where are they sent to? Are they sent to the cities? Because in the towns of the province of Ontario there is a dearth of domestic servants, we have never had one_ sent to our town. I venture to say that in the town I live in we could place 75 to 100 domestic servants. It is only fair, if the government pay bonuses on domestic servants, that the towns should get their proportion.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The question of domestic servants is a very serious and important one, and I may add a very difficult one. We have taken some means of dealing with the question of farm labour, but we have not taken the same measures in regard to domestic servants. There are difficulties in the way of handling the domestic servant question which lead me to hesitate at taking up a matter as a government responsibility. The domestic servants who are brought out as such come under the auspicies of certain societies, or of certain ladies who make a business of selecting servants in the old country, of fetching them out here, and of placing them after they get here. They are entitled to a bonus upon those servants after they have been placed in positions. But we do not

assume any responsibility or control of the movements of those servants, except that the person who claims a bonus upon them does not get the bonus unless the servant has been placed in domestic service. We do not undertake to say where the servants shall go. But as I say, there are difficulties in the way of handling domestic servants, and we have not undertaken to do more than offer these inducements, and to give as close supervision as we can to see that the work is not wrongly conducted.
To pay the balance due on rent of house leased for W. T. R. Preston while engaged as commissioner of immigration in London, Eng., $801.71.
Do you continue to pay rent for the successor of Mr. Preston?
